newsitem.title: ITALY: Turkey's Ciller slams EU, links issue to NATO.
newsitem.headline: Turkey's Ciller slams EU, links issue to NATO.

text.p: Foreign Minister Tansu Ciller on Tuesday bitterly criticised lack of progress on Turkey's bid for European Union membership and signalled that Ankara could block NATO's enlargement plans unless its aspirations are satisfied.

Speaking in Rome on the eve of talks with five key European colleagues, Ciller said Turkey was not seeking a special relationship with the 15-nation EU but would not be treated as a second-class associate.
"Either Turkey is a full member or she will not hang in as a second-rate member," Ciller, speaking in English, said in a speech to the Italian Institute of International Affairs.
Her speech drove home the bitterness Turkey feels at being excluded from a group of 11 countries which have officially joined the queue of aspiring new members.

Listing reasons why Turkey should be eligible to join, she said that "if it does not occur I feel it will be one of the largest mistakes of history because it will hurt the feelings of the Turkish people irreversibly and the choice will be made".

She made clear in a subsequent question and answer session that Turkey, a NATO member, could veto plans by the military alliance to expand into former communist eastern Europe unless the EU delivered on closer ties.
"How do you think you can expand NATO without Turkey's permission?" Ciller asked. "It cannot be separated, the expansion of Europe, the expansion of NATO, they are interlinked."

Ciller is due to meet in Rome on Wednesday with the foreign ministers of Britain, France, Germany, Italy and Spain for talks on Turkey's relations with Europe amid signs of growing strains on the EU issue and amid tensions with Greece over Cyprus.

The meeting is not technically in the EU framework and diplomats said Ciller was unlikely to receive any firm indication that Turkey's membership hopes would be met because the European Commission has yet to assess suitability.
"They'll be told we're waiting for the Commission. The EU has no position as yet," one diplomat said.
Turkey sees the EU's attitude as a hostage to Greek bias.

It also holds Greece responsible for blocking financial aid that was meant to have flown under a customs union which went into effect at the start of 1996, though there is also EU concern over Ankara's human rights record.

Cyprus and Malta have been told they can expect EU accession talks to start, probably in 1998, and nine countries from eastern and central Europe are to be judged on suitability to start negotiations.

"Now it is celebration time for the new Europe. Now the 15 have designated 11 more for potential new members. Everyone is in except for one country -- only Turkey. Only Turkey is left out," Ciller said.
On the tensions over Cyprus, Ciller told her audience that Turkey would "never initiate a crisis" over the divided island.
Greek Cypriot government plans to deploy Russian anti-aircraft missiles on the divided island have been met by Turkish threats of military retaliation.
Cyprus has been divided since 1974, when Turkey invaded and occupied the northern third of the island after a Greek Cypriot coup engineered by Greece's then military government.
